attempts.raw_response: The man he was speaking to smiled at this account of Parisian purchases and the tribulations of bringing them home. He inquired whether the pictures were modern works or older masters, and the gentleman explained that they had been recommended by a dealer as excellent investments, though he confessed he had little eye for such matters himself. His wife had particularly wanted a large landscape that dominated the drawing room, while his daughter had chosen a small portrait that now hung above the staircase. The artist or dealer—whichever he was—listened patiently to these details, occasionally nodding, and seemed amused by the man's frank admission that he could not tell one school of painting from another, but trusted entirely in the judgment of those who understood such things.

pair.human_continuation:
He mentioned the names of the artists who
had painted them, and asked Carstairs if he had ever heard of them,
and Carstairs said yes, that he knew of them all, and had studied
under some of them.

"They're purty high up, I guess," suggested the driver, tentatively.

"Oh, yes," Carstairs answered, lending himself to the other's point of
view, "you needn't be afraid of ever losing on your investment. Those
pictures will be worth more every year."

This seemed to strike the older man as a very sensible way to take his
gallery, and he said, when they had reached the studio, that he would
like to see more of Mr. Carstairs and to look at his pictures. His
name, he said, was Cole.
pair.prefix:
He asked him a great many questions about his work, and
told him that he owned several good pictures himself, but admitted
that it was at his wife's and daughter's suggestion that he had
purchased them. "They made me get 'em when we were in Paris," he said,
"and they cost a lot of money, and a heap more before I got 'em
through the Custom-house."

source_document.title: Van Bibber and Others by Richard Harding Davis
